meta.title: Chat Messaging
meta.summary: 1:1 and group messaging (WhatsApp / Messenger style) over persistent connections, with offline delivery, push notifications and encrypted media.

functional: Send photos, voice notes and files up to ~100 MB
Offline users get a push notification and receive missed messages on reconnect
Message history syncs across a user's devices
nonFunctional: Delivery < 500 ms when both users are online
No message is ever lost once the sender sees ✓
Messages appear in the same order for everyone in a conversation

scale.label: Media
scale.value: ~10% of messages carry a file (~4B/day, mostly < 1 MB)

slos.name: Delivery speed
slos.sli: Messages delivered to an online recipient within the threshold, divided by all such messages, from the Message Service receiving the send to the recipient's delivery receipt

slos.name: No message lost
slos.sli: Acknowledged messages that can still be read, divided by acknowledged messages, measured with canary conversations that send a message every minute from each zone and read it back later, plus repair checks on the store

slos.name: Connection availability
slos.sli: Connection attempts that complete the WebSocket upgrade, divided by all attempts, measured at the gateways (the NLB only sees TCP)

slos.name: Sending works
slos.sli: Sends acknowledged with ✓, divided by all sends, measured at the Message Service

alerts.when: Deliveries over 500 ms burning the latency budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Chat that is not instant feels broken.

alerts.when: Deliveries over 500 ms burning the latency budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: Gradual slowdown, often the registry or the store getting hot.

alerts.when: Send failures burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: People cannot send; nothing acknowledged is lost, but nothing new gets through.

alerts.when: Send failures burning the error budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: A slow leak of failed sends, often one store node or one zone.

alerts.when: Any canary message acknowledged but not readable afterwards
alerts.why: The one promise the product cannot break: an acknowledged message is gone.

alerts.when: Store write timeouts or unavailable errors at QUORUM above 0.1% for 5 minutes, or any store node down for 15 minutes
alerts.why: With one replica down every write still reaches quorum, but there is no margin left; a second failure in the same replica set stops sends.

alerts.when: Connection failures burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
Connection failures burning the error budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: Some users or networks keep failing to connect; often a bad gateway node or certificate.

alerts.when: Connections per gateway above 80% of the limit
alerts.why: Add gateways before a node hits its limit and drops its users.

alerts.when: Oldest push queue message above 60 seconds, or any message in the dead-letter queue
alerts.why: Offline users learn about messages late, or not at all.

alerts.when: Registered sessions differ from open connections by more than 2%
alerts.why: Messages get routed to gateways that no longer hold the user.

alerts.when: Gateway TLS certificate or push provider credentials expiring within 14 days
alerts.why: An expired certificate disconnects every user at once; an expired APNs key stops all iPhone pushes.

signals.name: Disconnects by reason
signals.why: Separates network problems from deploys and overload.

signals.name: Registered sessions against open connections
signals.why: Drift means stale entries or missed heartbeats.

signals.name: Write quorum failures
signals.why: The earliest sign that durability is at risk.

signals.name: Upload failures
signals.why: Shows whether signed URLs or storage are the problem.

signals.name: Messages sent and delivered per second
signals.why: Business view: the gap between sent and delivered is how much is waiting for offline users.

signals.name: Provider responses by code
signals.why: APNs 410 or FCM 404 (UNREGISTERED) means a stale token; 429 means APNs or FCM is throttling us.

steps: Open a slow delivery's trace: is the time in the store write, the session lookup or the gateway hop?
Check message store write latency and quorum errors.
Check the session registry: a missing entry sends the message down the offline path, a stale one to the wrong gateway.
Check gateway CPU and connection counts.
Check the push queue age, the dead-letter queue and worker errors.
Check provider responses: many unregistered tokens (APNs 410, FCM 404) mean stale device rows that need cleaning.
Check provider throttling (429) and that the APNs key and FCM credentials are still valid.
Check disconnects by reason: a deploy, one gateway node, or everything?
If one node, check whether it was drained or crashed; its users should reconnect elsewhere with backoff.
If everything, check the TLS certificate and the NLB, then watch the reconnect rate so the stampede does not overload the registry.

nodes.label: Network Load Balancer
nodes.description: Layer 4: passes long-lived TCP connections straight to the gateways; network DDoS protection, since an L4 balancer cannot carry a WAF

nodes.label: Chat Gateway
nodes.description: Terminates TLS and WebSockets; each node holds ~1M connections (an assumption to confirm with a load test), so ~200 nodes plus headroom

nodes.label: Message Service
nodes.description: Persists, routes and syncs messages (~2.8M operations/s at peak); gateways reach it by gRPC with client-side balancing across healthy instances

nodes.label: Session Registry
nodes.description: user → { device → gateway node }, refreshed by heartbeats with a short TTL

nodes.label: Message Store
nodes.description: Cassandra-style: partition = conversation, clustering = message id; also device rows with push tokens

nodes.label: Push Queue
nodes.description: Push jobs; dead-letter queue after 5 failed attempts

nodes.label: Push Workers
nodes.description: Calls APNs / FCM over the internet through the NAT gateways

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Answers with the region's NLB; short TTL so traffic can move

nodes.label: CDN (media)
nodes.description: Caches encrypted media near recipients, with a WAF attached; chat traffic never goes through it

nodes.label: WAF (media)
nodes.description: Rule set attached to the media CDN: managed rules, per-IP rate rules, bot control

nodes.label: Media Storage
nodes.description: Encrypted images, videos, voice notes and files

flows.title: Connect and go online
flows.summary: Resolve the service, open one long-lived connection, and register which gateway holds it so messages can find this user.

steps.label: resolve chat.example.com
steps.detail: Clients look the service up by name. A short TTL (about 60 s) lets traffic move to new load balancer addresses quickly. This happens once per connect, not per message.

steps.label: NLB address
steps.detail: Apps also ship a fallback hostname and a list of IPs, because DNS can be slow or blocked on some networks.

steps.label: TCP + TLS + WebSocket upgrade
steps.detail: One connection stays open for hours, so the cost of setting it up is paid once. The layer-4 balancer just passes the bytes through.
steps.payload:
GET /ws HTTP/1.1
Upgrade: websocket
Authorization: Bearer eyJ…

steps.label: pick a gateway (least connections)
steps.detail: Spreading connections evenly matters more than spreading requests: each gateway holds about a million sockets.

steps.label: authenticate + register phone-1
steps.detail: The gateway checks the token, then tells the Message Service this device is online here. The call goes by gRPC to any healthy Message Service instance; gateways balance per request on the client side, since a layer-4 balancer would pin long-lived HTTP/2 connections to one instance.

steps.label: HSET session:alice phone-1
steps.detail: This entry is how every later message finds each of Alice's devices. The gateway sends a heartbeat every 30 s, batched per gateway, that the Message Service turns into a refresh; if the gateway dies the key expires within a minute and she is treated as offline. Each field carries its own expiry time, so a dead laptop entry is ignored even while the phone keeps the key alive.
steps.payload:
HSET session:alice phone-1 "gateway-17 exp=1762600060"
EXPIRE session:alice 60

steps.label: connected
steps.detail: From here Alice can send and receive over the same socket. The client reconnects automatically with backoff and jitter, so a gateway restart does not cause a stampede.

flows.title: Send (recipient online)
flows.summary: Persist first, acknowledge the sender, then route to the exact gateway holding the recipient's connection.

steps.label: WS frame: send
steps.detail: The client generates its own message id so a resend after a dropped connection can be deduplicated.

steps.label: same TCP connection
steps.detail: A layer-4 balancer just pins connections; the gateway terminates the WebSocket.

steps.label: send
steps.detail: The gateway adds a trace id that follows the message through storage, routing and delivery, so one slow delivery can be traced end to end.
steps.payload:
send { conv_id: c_alice_bob, client_msg_id: a1-0042, device: phone-1 }
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01

steps.label: dedupe + INSERT (QUORUM)
steps.detail: Write before delivering: if anything crashes after this, the message still exists. A quorum write survives one replica being down. A resend with the same client_msg_id finds the first row and gets the same msg_id back, so it never duplicates; the read-then-write leaves a tiny race if two copies arrive at once, which the recipient's display dedupe covers.

steps.label: OK, msg_id
steps.detail: The server assigns the time-sortable msg_id, and every reader reads the same partition sorted by it, so everyone sees the same order.

steps.label: ack ✓
steps.detail: Internal RPC straight to the node that holds Bob's socket, by its address, not through any balancer. No broadcast to all gateways. If the node answers that Bob is no longer there (he reconnected elsewhere), the service falls back to the offline path.

steps.label: ✓ sent
steps.detail: Alice's single tick means: stored on the server, will not be lost.

steps.label: phone-1 on gateway-17
steps.detail: Bob's phone is online on gateway node 17. Each online device is delivered to the same way, and Alice's own other devices get a copy too; devices that are offline catch up on sync.

steps.label: deliver via gateway-17
steps.detail: Internal RPC straight to the node that holds Bob's socket, by its address, not through any balancer. No broadcast to all gateways. If the node answers that Bob is no longer there (he reconnected elsewhere), the service falls back to the offline path.

steps.label: new message
steps.detail: Bob's app places the message by its msg_id, so two messages arriving close together still show in stored order.

steps.label: delivered(msg_id)
steps.detail: Stored as a status on the message so Alice's other devices and a later sync see it, and relayed to Alice the same way, turning ✓ into ✓✓.

flows.title: Send (recipient offline)
flows.summary: Store, notify through APNs/FCM, and let the recipient pull missed messages when they reconnect.

steps.label: INSERT (QUORUM)
steps.detail: The message store is also the offline inbox: nothing extra to keep in sync.

steps.label: (none)
steps.detail: No heartbeat for 60 s, so the session key expired: none of Bob's devices is online.

steps.label: SELECT push tokens
steps.detail: Bob's devices and their push tokens are rows in the message store, written when each device registers.
steps.payload: SELECT device_id, push_token FROM devices WHERE user_id = 'bob';

steps.label: enqueue push
steps.detail: Push providers are slow and rate-limited; a queue keeps them off the send path. A job that keeps failing moves to the dead-letter queue.

steps.label: send notification
steps.detail: With end-to-end encryption the push carries no message text, just "New message" and a conversation id. The collapse id makes ten missed messages one notification. Calls leave the VPC through the NAT gateways.

steps.label: sync since cursor
steps.detail: The Message Service also registers Bob's device in the session registry again (not shown).

steps.label: SELECT msg_id > cursor
steps.detail: One partition read per conversation, already sorted by msg_id.

flows.title: Send an image
flows.summary: Media skips the chat servers: it goes straight to object storage with a short-lived signed URL, and the message carries only a reference. The recipient downloads it through a CDN.

steps.label: encrypt on device
steps.detail: The file is encrypted with a fresh random key before it leaves the phone. The key travels inside the end-to-end encrypted message, so storage and the CDN only ever see ciphertext.

steps.label: WS frame: request upload
steps.detail: Alice asks for an upload slot over her open connection.

steps.label: sign upload URL
steps.detail: The service signs a PUT URL locally with its storage credentials: it expires in 5 minutes and is bound to this size and content type. Nothing is sent to storage yet.

steps.label: upload slot
steps.detail: A 5 MB photo never touches the chat servers, which stay free for messages.

steps.label: PUT ciphertext (direct)
steps.detail: Gigabytes per second of uploads go straight to object storage. A failed upload is retried on its own, without resending a message.

steps.label: WS frame: send (media ref)
steps.detail: Now the ordinary message: text plus a reference to the file and its decryption key (inside the encrypted body).

steps.label: HEAD m/8c1f
steps.detail: Before accepting the message, check the file really arrived and its size matches. Otherwise Bob would get a message pointing at nothing.

steps.label: INSERT (QUORUM)
steps.detail: The message is stored like any other; only its body differs.

steps.label: ✓ sent
steps.detail: Delivery to Bob works exactly as in "Send (recipient online)" and is not repeated here.

steps.label: message arrives with a media reference
steps.detail: Bob sees a blurred thumbnail (sent inline in the message) while the full file downloads.

steps.label: GET /m/8c1f
steps.detail: Downloads use a plain HTTPS URL on the CDN, not the chat connection.

steps.label: inspect
steps.detail: The WAF on the media CDN applies managed rules and per-IP rate rules, so nobody can use the CDN to pull files in bulk. The files are ciphertext anyway; this protects cost and capacity.

steps.label: MISS
steps.detail: First recipient in this region. In a group chat, everyone after Bob gets a HIT, so the file leaves origin storage once.

steps.label: ciphertext
steps.detail: The CDN caches the ciphertext. It cannot read it, and storage lifecycle rules delete it after about 30 days.

steps.label: decrypt with the key from the message
steps.detail: Only Bob and Alice hold the key.

notes.text: Partition by conversation so one conversation's history is a single sorted read. Very large groups need bucketing (conv_id + month) to keep partitions bounded.
Quorum reads and writes across 3 zones keep working with one zone down; the cluster still has 2 of 3 replicas.

If a gateway node dies, its clients reconnect to another node and re-register. Messages sent in between wait in the store and arrive on sync. Sizing: ~200M sessions take only ~20 GB, but refreshing them every 30 s is ~7M writes/s, so the registry is a sharded cluster with dozens of shards, each with a replica in another zone; a longer heartbeat halves the load at the cost of slower offline detection.
WebSockets give instant delivery; long polling is simpler but costs far more requests. Gateways must drain connections gradually on deploys to avoid reconnect storms.

End-to-end encryption (Signal protocol): the server stores and routes ciphertext only and never sees message content. Gateways are the only public instances; the Message Service, registry and store sit in private subnets, the Message Service reaches media storage through a VPC endpoint, and the chat path relies on network DDoS protection at the NLB because a layer-4 balancer cannot carry a WAF.
Groups: small groups fan out on write (one delivery per member). Large broadcast channels switch to fan-out on read.

This design shows one region. DNS TTLs are short (about 60 s) so load balancer changes take effect quickly, and clients keep fallback hostnames and IPs. Serving users from several regions needs a home region per user or conversation and cross-region routing of messages, a larger extension than adding DNS geo routing.

Sending media through the chat servers would tie up gateway connections and bandwidth. Direct-to-storage upload with signed URLs scales independently, and multipart upload makes large files (up to ~100 MB) resumable.
Chat traffic is unique, long-lived connections, so a CDN cannot help there. It only serves media downloads, where one group photo is fetched by many recipients.

Order comes from the server-assigned time-sortable msg_id: everyone sees the same order because everyone reads the same sorted partition, but two messages sent within clock skew of each other may not be in true send order. A strict per-conversation sequence needs a single writer per conversation (route each conversation to one owner) or a lightweight transaction per message, which costs more at 460k messages/s.

questions.q: How do you keep messages in the right order within a conversation?
questions.a: Assign the order on the server when the message is stored, here a time-sortable msg_id, never the sender's clock, and have clients place messages by it. Everyone reads the same partition sorted by that id, so everyone sees the same order. A strict gap-free sequence per conversation would need one owner per conversation or a lightweight transaction, and ordering across conversations does not matter, which is what lets the store partition by conversation.

questions.q: Bob is offline when Alice sends a message. How does he get it?
questions.a: The message is stored first, so it is never lost. Because none of Bob's devices has a live entry in the session registry, a push job with his device tokens goes on the queue and the workers send it through APNs or FCM. When Bob opens the app it syncs everything after the last msg_id it saw in each conversation.

questions.q: How do you make sure a message is delivered exactly once even with retries?
questions.a: Delivery is at least once and display is exactly once. The client attaches a unique message id, the server keeps a lookup from that id to the stored message so a retry returns the same message instead of creating a duplicate, and the recipient ignores ids it has already shown. Acks for sent, delivered and read are separate events on the same id.

questions.q: With millions of connections across many gateways, how does a message find the recipient's connection?
questions.a: The session registry maps each online user's devices to the gateways holding their connections. The message service looks up Bob's gateway and calls that node directly. Entries are refreshed by heartbeats and expire so a dead gateway does not keep stale routes, and a node that no longer holds the user says so, which sends the message down the offline path.

questions.q: How does group chat change the design, especially for very large groups?
questions.a: Store a group message once and fan out only the delivery: look up members and push to those online, notify the rest. For large groups, avoid per-member writes and let clients pull by sequence number. Cap group size or switch very large groups to a broadcast or channel model.

questions.q: How are images and videos sent without overloading the chat servers?
questions.a: The sender uploads the file directly to object storage with a signed URL and the message carries only a reference and a small thumbnail. Recipients download it through the CDN. Chat servers only handle small messages, which keeps connection handling fast.
